question: A 3-year-old boy is taken to the ER by his parents due to his elevated temperature. He has had a fever (>101.1 deg F) for a little over a week, and over that time, his parents noticed his eyes had gotten a little pink, and his palms and soles were red and swollen. His lips and tongue are also peeling. His parents note he has not taken any new medications, and they did not notice any runny nose, sore throat, cough, or changes in his bowel or bladder habits. In the ER, his vitals are as follows: temperature is 101.3 deg F (38.5 deg C), blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 125/min, and respirations are 20/min. His exam is notable for bilateral injected conjunctivae, right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy, erythematous and edematous palms and soles, and erythema multiforme-like rash over his trunk. Appropriate lab tests and imaging were performed. Which of the following is the most worrisome complication of this boy's disease process?

enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of the 3-year-old boy, including prolonged fever, conjunctivitis, rash, swollen palms and soles, and peeling lips and tongue, is consistent with Kawasaki disease. The most worrisome complication of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysms, which can lead to significant cardiovascular issues. This aligns with the consensus that coronary artery aneurysms are the most serious and common complication associated with Kawasaki disease. Other potential complications like endocardial valve damage and digital gangrene are less common and not as immediately life-threatening. Glomerulonephritis and toxic epidermal necrolysis are not typically associated with Kawasaki disease. Therefore, the most worrisome complication in this context is coronary artery aneurysms.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 3-year-old boy is highly indicative of Kawasaki disease, characterized by prolonged fever, conjunctivitis, rash, swollen palms and soles, and peeling lips and tongue. Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis that primarily affects children and can lead to serious cardiovascular complications. The most worrisome complication associated with Kawasaki disease is the development of coronary artery aneurysms. These aneurysms can lead to myocardial infarction, ischemia, or sudden death, making them the most serious and life-threatening complication. Other options such as digital gangrene, endocardial valve damage, glomerulonephritis, and toxic epidermal necrolysis are either less common or not typically associated with Kawasaki disease. Therefore, based on standard medical knowledge and consensus, coronary artery aneurysms are the most concerning complication in this scenario.
